learning.title: A restore is not done until workers are fenced and restored skill bytes are read back
learning.trigger: Restoring a Bakery backup into a new or running installation, or declaring a backup procedure disaster-recovery ready.
learning.mistake: Restored the database dump and restarted every service, trusting live Redis, Inngest state and copied worker journals to match it, or counted a local-only backup or a passing checksum as a working restore.
learning.rule: PostgreSQL is the restored authority. Live Redis, Inngest state and worker journals form no common cross-service snapshot with it. Before resuming a business restore: stop the consumers, fence and re-enrol the workers, quarantine old active worker assignments and reconcile Inngest and Redis. Never replay a copied live worker journal against older database truth.

Logical dumps alone do not prove file and database alignment. The restore drill must read the skill bytes that the restored metadata references, before launch. A backup that never left its host is not disaster recovery: copy the encrypted artifacts off-host, and keep the private age identity off the host that took the backup.

Preserve the application secrets key and its id with the backup (see secrets-key-id-bound-into-ciphertext). Run restore drills in an isolated network-none container with no write to the production database; a destructive production restore needs a concrete incident plan and fencing of runtime sessions.

verification.command: sudo bash scripts/deploy/restore-check.sh <backup directory> <age identity file>
verification.requirement: It verifies hashes, decrypts, restores both databases with fail-on-error, checks user tables, extracts files and validates the release journal. Separately record a read of at least one restored skill object referenced by restored metadata.

learning.boundary: restore-check proves restorability of the encrypted artifacts, not a live recovery. Worker fencing and Inngest/Redis reconciliation are operator steps that no script performs.
